```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

This vignette describes the analysis of a proof-of-concept (PoC) study with
two continuous endpoints (Yamaguchi et al., submitted).
`vignette("two-binary")` describes the regions and the criteria for two
endpoints, which are the same here.

## Model

In group $k$ ($k = t, c$), the responses of a subject on the two endpoints
have a bivariate normal distribution $N_2(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)$, and the data
are summarized by the number of subjects, the vector of sample means and
the sample covariance matrix (`data_continuous2()`). With the
Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior (`prior_niw()`),
$$\mu_k \mid \Sigma_k \sim N_2(\mu_0, \Sigma_k / \kappa_0), \qquad
\Sigma_k \sim \textrm{Inv-Wishart}(\nu_0, \Lambda_0),$$
the posterior distribution has the same form with parameters
$(\mu_n, \kappa_n, \nu_n, \Lambda_n)$, and the mean has the bivariate t
distribution with $\nu_n - 1$ degrees of freedom, location $\mu_n$ and scale
matrix $\Lambda_n / \{\kappa_n (\nu_n - 1)\}$. With the vague prior
$p(\mu, \Sigma) \propto |\Sigma|^{-3/2}$ (`prior_vague()`), the posterior
distribution of the mean is $t_{n - 2}(\bar y, S / \{n (n - 2)\})$, where
$S$ is $n - 1$ times the sample covariance matrix.

For the predictive criterion, the mean of $m$ future subjects has the same
distribution with the scale matrix
$(1 / \kappa_n + 1 / m) \Lambda_n / (\nu_n - 1)$. Version 0.1.0 of the
package and Yamaguchi et al. (submitted) used
$(1 + \kappa_n) \Lambda_n / \{\kappa_n (\nu_n - 1) m\}$, which treats the
future subjects as independent draws from the predictive distribution of one
subject.

The treatment effects are $\theta_j = \mu_{tj} - \mu_{cj}$ ($j = 1, 2$), and
the probabilities of the regions are computed by one of two methods
(argument `method` of `design_continuous2()`):

- `"MM"` (the default): the difference of the two bivariate t
  distributions is approximated by a bivariate t distribution with matched
  moments (Yamaguchi, Homma, Takeda and Maruo, submitted, Theorem 3), whose
  rectangle probabilities are computed by numerical integration for real
  degrees of freedom; it requires more than 4 degrees of freedom in both
  groups;
- `"MC"`: Monte Carlo simulation with `nMC` draws from each distribution.

## Decision for observed data

The second case study of Yamaguchi et al. (submitted) has 30 subjects per
group, Normal-Inverse-Wishart priors, $\theta_{TV} = (10, 2)$ and
$\theta_{MAV} = (5, 1)$. Here the thresholds are
$\gamma_{go} = \gamma_{nogo} = 0.6$ (the article calibrates its own
thresholds):

```{r design}
L0 <- matrix(c(80^2, 15, 15, 6^2), 2, 2)
crit <- criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(10, 2), theta_mav = c(5, 1),
                            gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6)
des <- design_continuous2(
  n_t = 30, n_c = 30,
  prior_t = prior_niw(mu0 = c(0, 1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4, Lambda0 = L0),
  prior_c = prior_niw(mu0 = c(-10, -1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4,
                      Lambda0 = L0),
  criterion = crit
)
data_t <- data_continuous2(30, mean = c(12, 3),
                           cov = matrix(c(6400, 190, 190, 36), 2, 2))
data_c <- data_continuous2(30, mean = c(-10, -1),
                           cov = matrix(c(5600, 150, 150, 42), 2, 2))
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_t, data_c = data_c)
dec
```

The decision is `r dec$decision`. Monte Carlo simulation gives similar
probabilities of the regions:

```{r mc}
des_mc <- design_continuous2(
  n_t = 30, n_c = 30,
  prior_t = prior_niw(mu0 = c(0, 1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4, Lambda0 = L0),
  prior_c = prior_niw(mu0 = c(-10, -1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4,
                      Lambda0 = L0),
  criterion = crit, method = "MC", nMC = 10000
)
dec_mc <- qdm_decide(des_mc, data_t = data_t, data_c = data_c, seed = 1)
rbind(MM = dec$prob_regions, MC = dec_mc$prob_regions)
```

## Hypothetical control

For a study without a concurrent control group, `hypothetical(mean, r)`
gives the control mean the distribution of the treatment mean with location
`mean` and the scale matrix multiplied by `r`. The prior of the control
group is then not used and is left `NULL`:

```{r hypothetical}
des_hyp <- design_continuous2(
  n_t = 30, n_c = 0,
  prior_t = prior_niw(mu0 = c(0, 1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4, Lambda0 = L0),
  criterion = crit,
  hypothetical_c = hypothetical(mean = c(-10, -1), r = 1)
)
dec_hyp <- qdm_decide(des_hyp, data_t = data_t)
dec_hyp
```

## Fixed control

With `fixed_c`, the control means are known values, for example the means of
the standard of care reported in the literature. The probabilities of the
regions are then those of the bivariate t distribution of the treatment
mean, which are computed by numerical integration for any degrees of
freedom, so `method` is not used:

```{r fixed}
des_fix <- design_continuous2(
  n_t = 30, n_c = 0,
  prior_t = prior_niw(mu0 = c(0, 1), kappa0 = 0.1, nu0 = 4, Lambda0 = L0),
  criterion = crit, fixed_c = c(-10, -1)
)
dec_fix <- qdm_decide(des_fix, data_t = data_t)
dec_fix
```

The control means are not uncertain, so the probability of the Go region is
`r format(dec_fix$prob_go, digits = 3)`, compared with
`r format(dec_hyp$prob_go, digits = 3)` for the hypothetical control with
the same location.

## Operating characteristics

`qdm_oc()` simulates the sample means and the matrix of sums of squares and
cross-products of `nsim` studies under each scenario, with the same random
numbers for all scenarios. A scenario gives the means, standard deviations
and correlation of the two endpoints in each group. To keep this vignette
quick, 1000 studies are simulated per scenario (the default is 10000):

```{r oc}
effects <- expand.grid(theta1 = c(0, 10, 20), theta2 = c(0, 2, 4))
scen <- data.frame(mu_t1 = -10 + effects$theta1,
                   mu_t2 = -1 + effects$theta2, sd_t1 = 80, sd_t2 = 6,
                   rho_t = 0.3, mu_c1 = -10, mu_c2 = -1, sd_c1 = 80,
                   sd_c2 = 6, rho_c = 0.3)
oc <- qdm_oc(des, scen, nsim = 1000, seed = 1)
oc
plot(oc)
```

The simulation standard error of the probabilities is at most
$0.5 / \sqrt{nsim}$, `r format(0.5 / sqrt(1000), digits = 2)` for 1000
studies. The moment-matching approximation is much faster than Monte Carlo
estimation of the region probabilities, whose computing time is
proportional to `nMC` for every simulated study.

## Decision boundary

`qdm_boundary()` gives the decision on a grid of observed treatment means of
the two endpoints, for a given sample covariance matrix, and its plot shows
which means lead to Go, NoGo and Gray decisions. With a concurrent control
group, the observed control data are given by `data_c`, and the axes are the
observed differences in means:

```{r boundary}
b <- qdm_boundary(des, mean_t = list(seq(-30, 50, by = 2),
                                     seq(-3, 7, by = 0.25)),
                  cov_t = data_t$cov, data_c = data_c)
plot(b)
```

## Calibration of the thresholds

The thresholds are calibrated so that the Go criterion is met with
probability at most 0.1 when neither endpoint is improved, and the NoGo
criterion with probability at most 0.2 when the effects are 20 and 4:

```{r calibrate}
cal <- qdm_calibrate(des, scenario_go = scen[1, ], scenario_nogo = scen[9, ],
                     target_go = 0.1, target_nogo = 0.2, nsim = 1000,
                     seed = 1)
cal
plot(cal)
```

The calibrated thresholds add up to `r cal$gamma_go + cal$gamma_nogo`. When
the sum is 1 or less, a Go and a NoGo criterion can be met together (a Miss
decision); here Miss decisions have probability up to
`r format(max(cal$oc$Miss), digits = 2)` under the two scenarios, which the
warning reports. Larger thresholds also meet the targets, with more Gray
decisions: the design with $\gamma_{go} = \gamma_{nogo} = 0.6$ used above
meets the Go criterion with probability `r format(oc$Go[1], digits = 2)`
when neither endpoint is improved and the NoGo criterion with probability
`r format(oc$NoGo[9], digits = 2)` when the effects are 20 and 4, and Miss
decisions are impossible because the thresholds add up to more than 1.

continuous endpoints.

Yamaguchi, Y., Hu, H., Huang, Y., Han, C., Homma, G. and Wang, A.
(submitted). Bivariate Bayesian quantitative decision-making for two
endpoints in rare disease drug development.
